Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted

There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. author: Guardian Staff
description:
Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon

Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place (BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November).

The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies.
title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter

A legitimate concern is that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature in the NHS context, having been developed primarily for a very different US healthcare system.

During the French Revolution, 700 dance halls opened; in the 1830s, socialists liked dancing the galop because it involved changing partners; in 1968 (or thereabouts) women stopped letting men take the lead. “Dancing is like a carnival, freeing you from what you normally are,” Zeldin wrote. “Dancing together creates harmonies between people with different tastes. A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

The Gavin and Stacey actor, who made the comments while talking with female campmates on I’m a Celebrity, said: ‘You just can’t speak’

Joanna Page has spoken about an “awful” male actor who was “inappropriate” while they were working together. She explained that he would “whisper things in your ear” and sing chants about “what he was going to do to me”.

author: Flora Willson
description:
Bradford Arts Centre
Ian McMillan’s south Yorkshire language version of The Marriage of Figaro sets the opera in 1970s Bradford. Indian classical instruments join to the reworked score in this high-energy, low-budget and hugely enjoyable take

‘This will be better than Barnsley FC,” I overheard the poet, broadcaster and professional Yorkshireman Ian McMillan assuring a friend ahead of curtain-up on his dialect adaptation of Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro. “Everything’s better than Barnsley FC.”

I don’t know much about League One football, I admit, but this high-energy, low-budget production directed by Alex Chisholm for Bradford Opera Festival punches far above its weight and could definitely survive less self-deprecating comparisons.

author: Gerard Meagher
description:
• Interested clubs have until 1 February to come forward

  • Prem chief is in US attempting to find potential investors

Prem Rugby has fired the starting gun on expanding to 12 teams by formally asking interested clubs to come forward by February. The chief executive Simon Massie-Taylor is currently in the United States attempting to woo investors with the Prem determined to add two more teams to its ranks for the 2029-30 competition.

Previous top flight sides Worcester Warriors, who won last season’s rebranded Champ, and London Irish – who have signalled their intentions to return to the second tier as soon as next season – are among the clubs expecting to throw their hats into the ring while the Welsh Rugby Union has already sent a letter outlining a desire for clubs to join the Prem and create an Anglo-Welsh league.

title: Prem Rugby fires starting gun on 12-team expansion plan with £20m entry fee

author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
description:
Von der Leyen says she wants to give Kyiv ‘strong hand’ in talks and is confident all 27 member states will back idea

  • Europe live – latest updates

The EU executive has proposed a €45bn (£37.5bn) loan for Ukraine to help with a looming cash crisis and reinforce its defences, as Russia’s relentless bombardment continues.

Announcing the plan to lend Kyiv the money in 2027, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table. And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”

Continue reading...
title: EU proposes €45bn loan for Ukraine to avert cash crisis and boost defences

author: Interview by Imogen Tilden
description:
Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture

I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different.

Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first.

Continue reading...
title: A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot

author: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent
description:
Police are investigating death of child three days after emergency services were called to Cosy Toes nursery in Middleton

A three-year-old boy has died after a “medical emergency” at a nursery in Greater Manchester.

Emergency services were called to Cosy Toes nursery in Middleton, near Manchester on the afternoon of 2 November after “reports of a concern for a child”.

title: Boy, three, dies after ‘medical emergency’ at Greater Manchester nursery

author: Sandra Laville Environment correspondent
description:
Populations at lowest level on record with 45% of native breeding species in decline, environment regulator says

Environment secretary Angela Eagle, her ministers and Natural England are breaking the law by failing to intervene to slow the catastrophic decline of Britain’s wild birds, the UK’s environment regulator has said.

New data shows wild bird populations have dropped to their lowest level on record, with almost half – 45% – of 132 native breeding species in decline over a five-year period.

title: UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds

author: Guardian community team
description:
We’d like to hear from UK households about whether they’re switching energy suppliers to save money or finding that deals are too similar to make it worthwhile

Energy bills in Great Britain are forecast to rise by 26% from January, adding £443 to the typical household’s annual bill. The increase, driven by rising gas prices amid the Middle East conflict, would be one of the biggest quarterly rises on record, according to forecaster Cornwall Insight.

Are you shopping around for a better gas or electricity deal or have you decided to stay with your current supplier? What has influenced your decision?

author: Leah Harper
description:
From icy squirts to bed-bouncing vibrations, erotic hockey drama Heated Rivalry just got even raunchier in ‘extreme sensory’ 4DX cinema screenings. But one scene proved too much – even for the super fans

I’m in the cinema foyer when I first spot them: hockey jerseys. Lots of them. “I’ve no idea what to expect!” giggles Chloe, who is wearing a black and yellow “Rozanov” jersey. Like me, she has never been to a 4DX screening before – but when Cineworld announced it would be showing episodes five and six of queer hockey drama Heated Rivalry in the novel format, she booked tickets immediately. “I actually had tickets for the 2D screening, but cancelled them for this,” she says.

Over the last two weeks, Heated Rivalry fans have been treated to big screen marathons of Jacob Tierney’s hit TV show, based on Rachel Reid’s bestselling book series, Game Changers. But 4DX is next level. The “extreme sensory” cinema technology is usually deployed for high-octane action flicks – film
title: ‘I hope paramedics are on standby for the sex scenes!’ The wet and wild TV experience leaving fans dizzy

author: Tom Hunt
description:
Instant coffee granules are a great ingredient in baking, as shown in this sponge given extra depth from roast walnuts and cardamom-infused milk

It might taste subpar in the cup, but instant coffee is a great baking ingredient. Being dehydrated, it provides an intense coffee flavour without adding extra liquid, which often upsets the balance of a recipe. I don’t drink instant coffee myself, and the dregs of the jar we always seem to have at the back of the cupboard tend to grow old and stick together. They’re still good to use, though, and can be chipped off or even dissolved in the jar, if need be.

Continue reading...
title: How to turn the dregs of an instant coffee jar into a brilliant vegan cake – recipe | Waste not

author: Giles Richards in Las Vegas
description:
The Nasa astronaut is fast seeing the similarities between flying Artemis into lunar orbit and the Formula One team’s drive for sporting brilliance

There are characters aplenty within Formula One, a sport that attracts the larger-than-life, and at the sharp end can be a parade ground for swaggering egos. Yet the newest addition to the paddock is a man whose quietly spoken, understated thoughtfulness and insight is compelling. Now part of the Mercedes team, Reid Wiseman has been to the moon and with it brings a perspective like no other.

Wiseman was one of four astronauts, alongside Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, who completed the Artemis II lunar flyby in April. Last month Wiseman, the mission’s commander, became an ambassador for Mercedes’ F1 team, formalising a relationship that had been growing over several years, to the delight of his daughter Katey, a fan of newly crowned world champion Kimi Antonelli.
title: Reid Wiseman, the rocketman shooting for the moon in F1 with Mercedes

author: Matt Hughes
description:
The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster and the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry

The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but.

Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry.

Continue reading...
title: Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports

author: Sanya Mansoor
description:
Cair-Florida is suing state officials after designation meant it had to shut its doors to victims of harassment and discrimination

Omar Soboh, a student at the University of Florida, was organizing a campus panel about Islamophobia when he found out one of the groups being represented had suddenly been blacklisted by the state. Under a new process, Florida had designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights group, a domestic terrorist organization. The university’s Arab Students’ Association decided to cancel the event, and Soboh, who is Palestinian American, was disheartened.

“Our existence itself is political,” he said.

Continue reading...
title: This Muslim civil rights group defended pro-Palestine protesters. Then Florida labeled it a terrorist organization

author: Will Unwin
description:
Full-time defender and part-time model, the 31-year-old is happy to shine a light on both sides of his dual career

“I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and said: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds.

Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons.

title: ‘When I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West’: the two lives of Bromley footballer Omar Sowunmi

author: Tam Patachako
description:
Abdul Goni Gazi fainted with fear during his first big cat encounter but now his mission is to help them coexist with people

At the age of 15, Abdul Goni Gazi had an experience that would alter the course of his life. It began as a fishing trip with his brother, deep within the Sundarbans, a vast landscape of mangrove forest, rivers and islands stretching across the tidal delta of Bangladesh and India.

“We went to the riverbank to cut firewood for cooking,” he says. “I was standing there holding the boat in place, while looking towards the bank.”

Continue reading...
title: ‘When it roars, we roar back’: the man who faces Bengal tigers armed only with a stick

author: Daniel Harris
description:
ATP Finals updates, with play in Turin from 2pm GMT
Sign up and get The Recap newsletter | Email Daniel

One of the principal reasons we watch sport is because, unlike real life, we don’t know, with crushing and tedious inevitability, what’s going to happen. However that doesn’t feel like the case in men’s tennis at the moment: roughly, if Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz are healthy, one of them wins, but if they aren’t and it’s a tournament that really matters, Alexander Zverev wins.

And, if this week has shown us anything, it’s that this is even more the case now tan before. Zverev is 2-0 but more telling than that is the the manner of of his wins, neither Arthur Fils nor Ben Shelton able to so much as threaten him – and he has levels in reserve he’s not had to bother seeking.
title: Carlos Alcaraz v Daniil Medvedev: ATP Finals tennis group stage – live

author: Nina Lakhani
description:
She noticed the trees going first. Slowly she understood that the sea was going to take the whole village. This is Guadalupe Cobos Pacheco’s story

Location: El Bosque, Mexico

Disaster: Sea encroachment

The fishing village of El Bosque was the first community in Mexico to be recognised as climate-displaced. The inhabitants were moved in 2023. By then, coastal erosion and flooding had already taken many of the homes.

Continue reading...
title: ‘The sea washed away trees, then a whole row of houses. I knew it was time to get out’ – This is climate breakdown

author: Garth Cartwright
description:
He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original

‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.”

Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange
title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou

author: Andrew Lawrence
description:
After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement

I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech.

Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical
title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback

author: Press Association
description:
• Fly-half was cited for alleged unlawful tackle against Fiji

  • Rassie Erasmus had predicted player would be cleared

Ireland’s fly-half Sam Prendergast is available to face South Africa in the Nations Championship on Saturday after his citing for an alleged hip-drop tackle against Fiji was dismissed.

Prendergast was cited for the challenge on Fiji’s captain Peceli Yato under a new offence added to Law 9.13 at the start of November. However, following a hearing on Tuesday, an independent disciplinary committee decided no further action would be taken against the 23-year-old, who could have been hit with a suspension.

title: Ireland’s Prendergast free to face South Africa after avoiding hip-drop tackle ban

description:
After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs

When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI.

As per Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg, upon announcing the creation of a forum for players to share memories of sandpaper in South Africa eight years ago, two diametrically opposed versions of events can both be true.

author: Guardian community team
description:
We want to hear from people who own or run companies in Britain who are trying to hire under-25s. What obstacles do you face?

Labour’s long-awaited review into youth joblessness published this week recommended that ministers cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people.

Alan Milburn’s report into how to address the nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training in the UK also proposes setting up a youth opportunity service to provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work.

author: Olivia McEwan
description:
Wallace Collection, London
A sword, a wine cooler, a dazzling fresco … only a museum with such a copious store of treasures could put on a display this rich without having to borrow

Mounting a “store-cupboard” exhibition – choosing items from existing collections to make a new, contained display – can be a cheap and easy way for a museum to make something out of its existing resources, without the faff of securing loans or collaborating across the industry. In the case of the Wallace Collection, however, the store cupboard is so embarrassingly rich and diverse that strong displays such as this on Cosimo I de’Medici can be drawn from only a handful of its objects.

The 19th-century collection of Sir Richard Wallace holds a notable number of medieval objects, but their display can seem – at least to contemporary eyes – like a cacophony of applied arts, armour and paintings, not to mention a ton of gilt. This Medici display is part of a new enterprise d

author: Alice Speri
description:
With its policy priorities more mainstream than ever, the left is directing its momentum toward 2028

A week after the US midterms elections swept an unprecedented number of leftists into office across the country, about 600 people joined a Zoom call. The goal: to convince rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president.

On the call, organizers from Ready for AOC, a new group of progressive and labor organizers, wasted little time celebrating the Democrats’ electoral sweep. “People all over the country are ready for a much different and much better future,” said Genevieve Rand, an organizer with the group. “We are more ready than we have ever been.”

title: Fresh off recent wins, the left has a new goal: get AOC to run for president

author: Kim Heacox
description:
Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves

Imagine traveling nonstop for 49 years, alone in the dark with no destination in sight, powered by curiosity and engineering.

Further imagine making that journey not at bullet train or jet plane speed, but much faster: at 37,800 miles per hour, free from friction in a vast sea of cold, soundless space, bombarded by radiation and cosmic rays yet still able to communicate with folks back home.

Continue reading...
title: After 49 years, Nasa’s Voyager 1 is one light-day away from us. Can we save this ‘pale blue dot’? |

The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares

Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while, and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down.

description:
With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre

In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. The energy company SSE has warned it will close its Atwick natural gas storage facility in northern England next summer, if the government does not intervene to offer support amid weak market conditions.

description:
Bored of red and gold? This year’s tree trimmings are felted, beaded and handmade – and they’re all glitter-free

• The best artificial Christmas trees – tested

Baubles: every time we think we’ve reached peak wackiness, we’re proved wrong the following year. author: Emily Woof
description:
Before an assassination attempt on Andy Warhol in 1968, Solanas used her fierce writing to confront male supremacy. What can her work teach us about expressing raw anger?

It is exhausting to always express anger constructively and reasonably – especially when what you are angry about is violence, exploitation and the inexcusable appetite of disgusting, powerful, greedy men to gain yet more power.

Could you please be more balanced in how you express yourself? Could you make your objection to the destruction of the world – through violating not only women but also the planet – well, more constructive? Could you be a little less unpleasant in your anger?

title: Valerie Solanas’s obscenely funny Scum Manifesto is an unignorable burst of female outrage | Emily Woof

author: Exclusive by Matt Hughes
description:
• Controversial breaks were financial boon for broadcasters

  • Fifa flags possible benefits but says no decision made

Fifa’s tender documents for TV rights for the 2030 World Cup includes a provision for broadcasters to sell adverts during hydration breaks in a strong indication the controversial stoppages will be retained.

A three-minute break midway through each half was introduced for the first time at all 104 matches at last summer’s World Cup in the interests of player welfare, a radical move that also provided a commercial boon for broadcasters, particularly the rights holders in the United States, Fox Sports and Telemundo.

title: Fifa’s World Cup TV rights documents indicate hydration breaks will stay in 2030

author: Guardian sport
description:
• Test batter felt ‘betrayed and alone’ after Cummins’ comments

  • He says ball-tampering agent discussed by players and coaches in 2018

Former Test cricketer Cameron Bancroft has claimed the entire Australia team knew about the use of sandpaper during the 2018 South African tour, where he was caught on video with the item in his hand in Cape Town and was later one of three players banned.

Bancroft alleged bowlers provided feedback on his attempts to alter the ball and a coach instructed him to do more, in a column written for the West Australian.

description:
Former foreign secretary’s intervention comes as prime minister prepares for major UK-EU summit in Brussels

David Lammy has urged Andy Burnham to campaign on a promise to rejoin the EU at the next election.

The former foreign secretary, who also served as deputy prime minister under Keir Starmer, said the prime minister’s Liverpool conference speech “blew the door wide open” on the issue.

title: David Lammy urges Andy Burnham to campaign on rejoining EU at next election

author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
description:
Government under pressure to help households as increase would add £443 to average annual dual-fuel bill

  • UK inflation rises to 3.6% after petrol and diesel prices hit record high

  • Business live – latest updates

Energy bills across Great Britain are predicted to reach £2,166 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East conflict piles pressure on the government to offer more support to hard-hit households.

description:
As a researcher for the Milburn review, I’ve seen how we’ve failed a generation – then castigated them. Britain must break this vicious cycle

Alan Milburn and Peter Fonagy have, between them, expertly diagnosed the UK’s illness. Their reviews show we don’t just have a Neet crisis. Or a school absence crisis. Or a Send crisis. We have a neglected childhood crisis that will wreck the country’s long-term pr

author: Darren Richman
description:
With the UK release of You Can See Everything looming, now’s an ideal time to get up to speed on the bizarre, puckish and very meta comedic oeuvre of its star

“There are three sides to every story: your side, my side, and the truth. And no one is lying. Memories shared serve each differently.” Those words were spoken by film producer Robert Evans – but nobody has ever interrogated the idea more skilfully than comedian Nathan Fielder.

The three-hour documentary You Can See Everything – co-directed by and starring Fielder – opens in the UK on Friday, having already become an unlikely cultural phenomenon and box office sensation in the US. To view the film as being simply about the Theranos scandal is akin

author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
description:
Increase in October piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy

Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October after petrol prices rose and diesel hit a record high amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East.

author: Ajit Niranjan
description:
Few signs of progress since draft deal exposed disagreements over what countries are willing to do stop the planet heating

Good morning, I’m Ajit Niranjan bringing you the Cop31 liveblog from Berlin. We’re heading into the final hectic days of negotiations, and my colleagues on the ground will be guiding you through the conclusion of these contentious climate crisis talks.

Delegates arrived to the Cop31 conference centre under grey skies and showered by a fine drizzle this morning. The weather could have been straight from a school creative writing piece, for these are the final days when the UN climate talks get serious.

title: Cop31 live: clock running down on climate talks as deep divisions remain

author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
description:
Research to look at whether ban can make meaningful change in mental health and wellbeing for under-16s

Countries around the world are considering social media bans for children, but whether this would work in practice has been hotly debated. Now researchers are seeking answers through a major scientific study led by Wellcome, which will be the first of its kind.

Ten research projects will explore topics ranging from children’s mental health to their sleep and physical activity, comparing factors before and after the social media ban for children under 16 is introduced in the UK in spring 2027.

Continue reading...
title: £10m ‘once-in-a-generation’ study to explore effects of children’s social media ban

author: Sandra Haurant
description:
More people take pet insurance than income protection policies but here are plans worth considering

No one wants to spend time imagining the worst thing that could happen, and perhaps that is why about 60% of UK adults have no life insurance, or why more people have pet insurance than have income protection for if they become too sick to work

However, there are certain milestones in life, such as having children or taking on a mortgage, that focus the mind on what might happen if things do go wrong. How would your family manage if you or your partner died? How would you cover the mortgage if you had an accident and couldn’t work?

title: Life insurance: do you have a safety net to protect you and your family if the worst happens?

author: Andrew Roth, Global affairs correspondent
description:
As Ukraine’s capital suffers through an energy crisis, many blame Vitali Klitschko for failing to prepare for winter

Maksym Bakhmatov, the outspoken head of one of Kyiv’s largest city districts, did not mince his words when it came to who was responsible for the devastating power outages plaguing his area’s 600,000 residents.

“First, because of Putin,” he said from his office in Desnianskyi, a working-class area on Kyiv’s left bank. “Second, because of lack of normal management from the mayor, [Vitali Klitschko]. That’s it.”

Continue reading...
title: Russian attacks have left Kyiv with devastating power outages – and its mayor in a perilous position

author: Lucy McGuire
description:
Heritage railways will soon be steaming into action, with special departures offering winter landscapes, seasonal goodies and a chance to meet Father Christmas

Red tablecloths, festive decor and tartan upholstered carriage seats bring the yuletide vibe onboard Strathspey Railway’s Elf Express. From your first-class carriage of either a steam-hauled or heritage diesel engine, you will be served sandwiches and cakes from traditional tiered plates, washed down with hot drinks and fizz. Santa and his elves will visit your carriage with presents for children, otherwise sit back and enjoy the woodland and moorland scenery of rural Speyside on this 20-mile round-trip (lasting about 1 hour and 40 minutes) between Aviemore and Broomhill.
Weekends and select weekdays until 24 December, £260 for four people.

Continue reading...
title: Dashing through the snow: 10 of the UK’s best Christmas train rides

author: Rob Cameron in Prague
description:
Večerníček has wished children goodnight for 60 years, and now his distinctive newspaper hat symbolises the fight for the future of public broadcasting

Photos of the mass rallies in support of Czech public broadcasters in recent weeks have featured one detail that has baffled outsiders: demonstrators wearing little hats made out of folded newspapers.

But to Czechs they are instantly recognisable. The hat belongs to Večerníček, a little cartoon boy who appears on Czech Television every evening at 6.45pm.

Continue reading...
title: The voice of a nation: the Czech children’s TV show that became a symbol of media freedom

author: Guardian Staff
description:
He’s shot Kate Moss and Kurt Cobain – and even dealt with Frankenstein’s monster. A new exhibition traces the British photographer’s evolving journey

Continue reading...
title: Nietzsche, the supermodels and me: the dazzling career of David Sims – in pictures

author: Luca Turin
description:
Scientific discoveries are effortlessly explained in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by passion

Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work.

But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood.
title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
The Oscar-winner plays a Muslim contract killer in a boisterous, blackly comic thriller with shades of John Woo and Tarantino

There are shades of John Woo and Tarantino here in a black-comic thriller from Pakistani-American director Bassam Tariq. There are shades also of Blade, the Marvel character that this film’s star, Mahershala Ali, had been preparing to play in a planned but then cancelled MCU movie which Tariq was going to direct. Here Ali plays Latif, a military veteran turned hitman for hire who uses knives and swords, not guns, and just happens to be a devout Muslim. The title refers to the Islamic tradition in which Muhammad was asked three times who is the most deserving of respect and replied each time: “Your mother.” It is, however, this film’s semi-intentional irony that mothers and female authority figures are largely irrelevant in it, the drama being more about men wi
title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother review – Mahershala Ali’s religious hitman on the hunt for baby milk

author: Ioan Marc Jones
description:
At a restaurant in Italy in 2022, every forkful of my meal made my eyes close and mouth water. For four years since, I have tried to recreate this dish. The pursuit has finally made me a proper vegetarian

I’ve ostensibly been vegetarian for 13 years and, in that time, I’ve eaten a lot of meat. My mum used to leave out the last bit of lamb madras, with a wink, then loudly announce that she was going to bed. I have accidentally found myself in KFC at midnight, hood up, drunk, looking both ways and asking for a Bargain Bucket. My partner once came home early from a night out and caught me red-handed, in bed with McDonald’s Chicken Selects. Such incidents were infrequent moments of weakness and, after the fact, I was always racked with guilt. But for most of my vegetarian life, I had felt a certain emptiness; a gaping meat-shaped hole in my heart and stomach.

Then I ate a bowl of pasta. It was 2022 and an Italian university friend, Mattia, invited me to Tuscany. I spent fou
title: A moment that changed me: the tomato pasta that became an obsession – and helped me lead a better life

author: Michael Segalov
description:
The documentary has triggered fierce backlash, but by exposing the army’s conduct in Gaza it’s proved impossible to ignore

It was on Yom Kippur this year that Nadav Weiman first sensed the documentary NAZA was having a significant impact in Israel – despite the fact that back in September, when the Jewish festival fell, barely a handful of Israelis had seen the film.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and will stream for free on its website in early December, depicts 24 army intelligence officers interviewed anonymously on rooftops across Tel Aviv. They talk about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza over the past three years, and the secret signoff system employed by Israel’s military. More than 1.5 million people have alre
title: ‘They want silence’: how the film NAZA is shaking Israel

author: Phil Harrison, Hannah Verdier, Hollie Richardson and Simon Wardell
description:
This two-parter follows the police investigation in the aftermath of the 2017 fire. Plus, father and son go on a double date in First Dates. Here’s what to watch this evening

9pm, BBC Two
“I awoke and the whole room had exploded,” recalls Bex Williams of New Year’s Day 2017, when she was the victim of an arson attack. Bex survived to tell the tale but, tragically, her boyfriend Cameron Logan died. This visceral two-part documentary tells the story of the aftermath, including Bex’s long recovery and the police investigation which concentrated on a brotherly feud. Phil Harrison

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: the terrifying and tragic case of a New Year’s Day arson attack

author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
description:
Campaign groups and regulators say data breaches are distressing for patients and families and erode trust in the health service

The NHS in England has recorded more than 3,000 incidents of staff inappropriately snooping on patients’ medical records in the last five years.

Patient campaign groups and regulators said the figures were “deeply concerning” and distressing for patients and families, and eroded trust in the health service. A lack of transparency from NHS organisations after data breaches were uncovered further compounded the heartache, they added.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Deeply concerning’: NHS in England reports more than 3,000 incidents of staff snooping on patients’ records

author: Neha Gohil Midlands correspondent
description:
Party promised a Musk-inspired blitz at councils in England, but research shows it has failed to cut harder or faster than comparable local authorities

When Reform UK secured a historic breakthrough in the May local elections last year, it was – according to the party leader, Nigel Farage – time for the UK to emulate Donald Trump and make sweeping local government cuts.

At the time, the US president had enlisted the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, to run his “department of government efficiency” (Doge). During a 16-week blitz at the heart of the US government, Musk caused chaos, fired tens of thousands of workers and gutted USAID.

Continue reading...
title: ‘In the end, nothing happened’: how Reform’s Doge-style crackdown fell flat

author: Romy Gill
description:
Spiced prawns cooked in coconut milk and a whole roast cauliflower with almonds and coriander – these dishes take me back to the food of my childhood

These two dishes are just the kind of food I want to eat on a chilly evening. The cauliflower is deeply spiced, nutty and comforting, with coconut, almonds, ginger and chilli bringing warmth and texture, while the prawn masala is quicker and lighter, but still full of flavour, with the spices and the sweet prawns coming together beautifully. Both dishes reflect the way I love to cook: generous, vibrant with layers of spice, but never so much that you lose the character of the main ingredient.

Continue reading...
title: Prawn masala and spiced roast cauliflower: Romy Gill’s Indian recipes for chilly nights

author: Rafael Behr
description:
In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours

In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power”.

Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist
title: Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe | Rafael Behr

author: Robyn Vinter North of England correspondent
description:
Lasting cross-class friendships involve routinely ‘taking the piss’ out of the more privileged party, research by the LSE shows

Routinely “taking the piss” out of more privileged friends is one of the main ways people cope with a class difference in their friendships, research has found.

Cross-class friendships are widespread and mutually beneficial, a study by the London School of Economics showed, but a class gap can still pose an “omnipresent threat” to friendships.

Continue reading...
title: How to deal with a class difference in friendships? Make fun of your privileged friends

author: Claire Stares
description:
Eyjafjörður: Our boat was surrounded by around 15 of them, exploding their exhalations out of the water – and numbers are increasing here

For the first half-hour, Eyjafjörður, Iceland’s longest fjord, offered few signs of marine life – just three cormorants and a raft of common eiders. Then, suddenly, there it was. A distant spout of water vapour. A humpback whale.

As we motored out, more bushy plumes appeared to port and starboard, until we found the boat surrounded by about 15 individuals. Cutting the engine, the captain announced that he was about to employ a secret technique to coax the whales closer. There were raised eyebrows as the opening notes of Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On crackled over the speakers. But, as if on cue, two explosive exhalations erupted alongside the boat, prompting whoops of deli
title: Country diary: Thrilling views of Iceland’s humpbacks, (perhaps) lured in by Céline Dion | Claire Stares

author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
description:
Meaning and use of word has become more important in age of AI chatbot, says dictionary

In a world where the line between people and machines is more blurred than ever, Cambridge dictionary has sided with natural intelligence for its word of the year: human.

Breakthroughs in artificial intelligence – led by the arrival of ChatGPT three years ago – have made the question of what it means to be human as vexed as ever, but the dictionary has drawn a firm line with its choice of the word of 2026, defining “human” as “having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines”.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Human’ wins Cambridge dictionary’s word of the year

author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
description:
Experts call trial results of medication that slowed cognitive decline by almost a third ‘very promising’

A pill that mimics Viagra by relaxing blood vessels and increasing blood flow to the brain can slow cognitive decline in people with Alzheimer’s disease by almost a third, a global study suggests.

Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, a condition that is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050. There is currently no cure.

Continue reading...
title: Pill that mimics Viagra can slow Alzheimer’s progression, study suggests

author: Elle Hunt
description:
How did Hollywood’s most eccentric star get cast in its most mainstream role? Here is all the bizarre and baffling lore from his lustrous career

It’s bad news for Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor, of course, but the announcement that Robert Pattinson will be the next 007 means that those people who have never cared much about James Bond finally have a reason to.

The appointment has been greeted with much excitement by everyone who has had a soft spot for R-Patz since Twilight, the sense-defying sparkly vampire franchise that transformed him into a reluctant teen heart-throb and household name.

Continue reading...
title: The first truly weird Bond: 13 things to know about Robert Pattinson – from heavy saliva to dead clowns

author: Mark Townsend
description:
New assessment shows large increase in cases where access to humanitarian help is deliberately restricted in conflict zones, with most incidents in Palestine

The “weaponisation” of aid is becoming normalised, with new analysis revealing that deliberate holding back of humanitarian help to children in conflict zones has increased 16-fold in the past decade.

The assessment of UN-verified incidents corroborates concerns that denying vital aid is becoming a common tactic of modern warfare.

Continue reading...
title: Cases of children being denied aid in war zones are soaring, analysis finds

author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
description:
Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

Continue reading...
title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt

author: Joseph de Weck
description:
French teachers argue that a digital detox woke students up to the decrepit state of their schools – and drove them out into the streets

Remember the 1999 blockbuster The Matrix? It may be more than a quarter of a century old, but it has become a byword and a meme for a frighteningly plausible kind of 21st-century tech dystopia.

A quick recap: the computer hacker Neo discovers that machines rule over humanity. They keep people trapped in pods, their minds immersed in a virtual reality designed to keep them docile (the “Matrix” of the title). Once he becomes aware of the world he actually inhabits, Neo decides to take up arms.

Continue reading...
title: Macron banned smartphones in schools. A month later, France was ablaze. Could they be connected? | Joseph de Weck

author: Emine Saner
description:
In her new film, the actor plays a lawyer taking on the French state over reproductive rights. She talks about being criticised for her support of Israel and pushed to the limit by Lars von Trier

While she was making the film Women on Trial, about the real-life trial of a child prosecuted for having an abortion, someone sent Charlotte Gainsbourg a photograph of her mother at one of the pro-choice demonstrations that erupted in France at the time. It was “very moving”, says Gainsbourg to see her mother, the actor Jane Birkin, in 1972, “looking beautiful and in the middle of a demonstration”. At that time, in a court in Bobigny, a Paris suburb, the prominent lawyer Gisèle Halimi was defending 16-year-old Marie-Claire Chevalier, as well as her mother and two other women who he
title: ‘The aesthetics in my family were so high, I felt ugly’: Charlotte Gainsbourg on extremism, abortion and her mother, Jane Birkin

author: Hanad Ahmed
description:
Research also shows consuming wine could cut risk, reopening debate on whether beverage has health benefits

Drinking beer and spirits increases the risk of serious kidney damage, whereas consuming wine offers protection against it, a study suggests.

People who drink nine units of spirits a week are 26% more likely to suffer acute kidney injury than those who consume only one unit a week.

Continue reading...
title: Drinking beer and spirits raises risk of acute kidney damage, study suggests

author: Kate Lamb
description:
Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin

  • Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit

  • What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds

President Xi Jinping addressed the Apec CEO summit this morning. His speech called for the elimination of trade and investment barriers, as well as greater cooperation around artificial intelligence.

He also emphasised the importance of the World Trade Organization, and said China was expanding its imports of quality goods and services.

We should not only eliminate trade and investment barriers... but also promote inclusive and balanced development.

We should actively build p
title: Apec summit live: Xi and Putin give opening speeches as world leaders gather in China

author: Guardian sport and agencies
description:
• No further sanctions expected regardless of findings

  • ‘The perfect truth doesn’t exist,’ says CEO Todd Greenberg

Cricket Australia will set up an independent forum to create a “safe space” in which players and staff can share their experiences of the sandpaper scandal, but the governing body does not expect to issue any further sanctions, regardless of what is learned from the process.

CEO Todd Greenberg and interim chair David Boon faced the media on Wednesday before the start of the third ODI against England in Hobart. Boon said the latest furore is damaging the game, but the new initiative “is not about re-litigating the past”.

Continue reading...
title: ‘The game is hurting’: Cricket Australia creates forum for players to air views on sandpapergate

author: Martin Pegan (now) and Rob Smyth (later)
description:
• Updates ahead the final ODI in the series at Bellerive Oval

  • Play start time in Hobart is 2.30pm AEDT/3.30am BST

  • Any thoughts? Get in touch with an email

We are indeed very, very proud the culture that this team has built the past eight years. Our players our leaders, our coaches deserve enormous credit for that. In particular Pat and Andrew who continue to lead this team with distinction. But we recognise the pain and the hurt that events surrounding sandpaper have caused. The game is genuinely hurting the moment. It’s not good for anyone. We need to find a path through, we need some time to heal.

As of this process, and so all parties who wish to can tell their version of events we have set up now an independent forum, a chance to give everyone a voice in an independent a safe setting. It’s not investigation. It’s not to produce a sanction. No one is forced to participate.
title: Cricket Australia to create forum for players and staff to share views on ‘sandpapergate’ – live

author: Justin McCurry in Tokyo
description:
Under pressure from Donald Trump, Japan’s government could be about to lift a ban on imported American potatoes, which famers say would threaten their livelihoods

It could be a piping hot croquette eaten on the go, a bowl of nikujaga stew or a plate of home-cooked chips. One culinary thread runs through them all – the Japanese potato.

Along with rice, the crop is fiercely protected as one of only a few homegrown staples in a country that imports more than 60% of its food.

Continue reading...
title: A potato war has been simmering for decades between the US and Japan. It’s about to reach boiling point

author: Reuters
description:
Asif Merchant, allegedly linked to Iran, found by court to have sought retribution over Qassem Suleimani death

A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said.

Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found.

Continue reading...
title: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years in US prison over Trump murder plot

author: Nadeem Badshah
description:
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is charged with destruction of US government property, after allegedly cutting hydraulic lines

An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked at an Irish airport, US prosecutors said.

Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is accused of cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks.

Continue reading...
title: Man accused of destroying US military plane at Shannon airport in Ireland

author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
description:
After damning report into standards at the top of forces in England and Wales, 200 people a year with superintendent potential to be recruited

Hundreds of people will be trained to boost “frankly inadequate” leadership of law enforcement, the home secretary is to say.

Shabana Mahmood will tell police chiefs and leaders at their central London annual conference on Wednesday that standards must improve as she unveils a scheme to train 200 people a year, after a report in June into police leadership found it was at times “staggeringly” poor.

Continue reading...
title: Shabana Mahmood to launch fast-track training to improve police leadership

author: Jasper Jolly, Jillian Ambrose and Kiran Stacey
description:
Analysts say mooted move to let more petrol and diesel vehicles be sold would wreck plan to reach net zero by 2050

Weakening the UK’s electric car sales rules would probably cause the government to miss legally binding climate targets, according to advisers tracking Britain’s progress to net zero.

The analysis by the Climate Change Committee (CCC) suggests the policy would blow a hole in the plan for achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 – prompting concerns that Andy Burnham’s government will have to slash the UK’s carbon emissions reduction targets, known as the carbon budgets.

Continue reading...
title: UK will miss climate targets if it weakens EV sales rules, advisers warn

author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
description:
CBI says restrictions on cross-Channel work trips are hindering investment and trade between UK and Europe

Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips.

A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week.

Continue reading...
title: Brexit work travel rules need urgent improvement, say UK business leaders

author: Richard Adams Education editor
description:
England’s exam regulator says those caught using AI or smart glasses face disqualification from GCSEs and A-levels

Students in England could suffer “life-altering” penalties if they are caught relying on AI or smart glasses to cheat, England’s qualifications regulator has said.

The head of Ofqual, Ian Bauckham, said students could be disqualified from GCSEs, A-levels and other qualifications if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework, and called for retailers to be barred from marketing wearable technology for exam cheating.

Continue reading...
title: Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat
